transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2028-10-04
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Camber Head of Security), Leah Ortiz (CTO), Priya Singh (Platform Lead), Daniel Knox (Compliance)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on residency constraints, logging retention and redaction, and whether Redwood Hosted with fallbacks or a Dedicated/Private deployment fits Camber's financial services controls. Customer cares about EU residency, SOC2 evidence, KMS/HSM key custody, and the ability to scrub/tokenize PII in logs.

Topics:
- Hosting options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
- Data residency (EU-UK region requirements)
- Log retention, redaction, and access controls
- Keystore/KMS and escrow needs
- Fallback routing and auto-failover for compliance boundaries

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, I'm your AE, joining with Maya our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Samir Rao: Good, thanks. Quick note: we're trying to map out the hosting fit for a new customer-facing assistant. Has to run with strict EU data residency and additional audit lines.
[00:22] Leah Ortiz: Yeah, the product team is strapped for time. The question is: do we go Redwood Hosted for speed, or Dedicated/Private to meet the controls—what's the trade off.
[00:35] Alex Chen: Totally. Maya, want to jump in on the architecture differences quickly?
[00:38] Maya Patel: Sure. So high level, hosted is quickest — we host in your region, you call the API, tokens billed. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with isolation, and Private means a customer-controlled VPC with private control plane. For residency: we can pin model endpoints to EU regions, we also support private deployments for on-prem or VPC.
[00:55] Daniel Knox: When you say pin, do you have hard region locks? We need to prove no cross-border token egress for GDPR regs.
[01:03] Maya Patel: We have region lock capabilities — we can ensure inference nodes and control plane stay within the EU region for a given tenant. For Hosted we do regional tenancy; for Dedicated it's a single-tenant GPU pool in the region. For Private you control the control plane in the VPC so there's no outbound egress to other regions.
[01:22] Samir Rao: Ok, and audit evidence — we need SOC2 or ISO attestation. Also technical artifacts like network diagrams, flow of data, and audit log samples.
[01:31] Alex Chen: We can share our SOC 2 Type II report and a redacted network diagram. I'll attach those after.
[01:36] Leah Ortiz: Another thing — key custody. Our compliance team wants HSM-backed KMS, and ideally a customer-owned key for encryption at rest. Can you route keystore calls to our KMS?
[01:47] Maya Patel: Yes, we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations. On Hosted we can integrate with the cloud provider KMS in your account, or for Private we can use your on-prem HSM. There's also a key-escrow flow if required for legal holds.
[02:02] Priya Singh: How about logs — we are required to retain request logs for 7 years for certain products, but the logs must be redacted for PII and only accessible to a small group. What's Redwood's logging model?
[02:14] Maya Patel: By default Redwood captures request metadata and token-level usage for billing and observability; we can configure log retention windows per-tenant, and have redaction hooks. We offer token-level cost breakdown and optional capture of prompts. For your case we recommend caching/scrubbing at the edge — prefix/KV- cache can reduce token capture and we can apply automated PII scrubbing pre-ingest.
[02:37] Samir Rao: When you say redaction hooks, is that automatic or a manual step? We need deterministic redaction so we're not storing unmasked PANs or SSNs.
[02:45] Maya Patel: There's two layers — pre-ingest filters you can run in your stack before it hits our control plane; and server-side scrubbing where we run regex-based redactors and a tokenization pipeline. Neither is perfect but together they meet most compliance needs. We sometimes see transcription of 'VPC' as 'V P C'—sorry bad example, but, yeah, regex needs tuning.
[03:02] Daniel Knox: Do you support differential retention? For example, redact prompt contents but keep metadata like route, model, time, and a hashed user id.
[03:12] Maya Patel: Yes, we can separate the metadata channel from the content channel. We can keep metadata for tracing and retain it longer while the full prompt content is redacted or shortened. We also support hashing user ids and tokenizing sensitive spans.
[03:26] Leah Ortiz: There's also a legal requirement in some of our jurisdictions to have local-only keys — the key never leaves the EU, even for emergency access. Will that be possible?
[03:35] Maya Patel: With Private deployments or a Dedicated hosted in your EU cloud account we can ensure the KMS/HSM stays in-region and keys do not leave. For Hosted managed by Redwood we'd need to use provider KMS in the EU region or integrate with your account.
[03:48] Priya Singh: How about fallback routing? Say our primary EU region hits capacity — what's the failover behavior? We can't allow requests to be served outside the EU.
[03:58] Alex Chen: Important point. Redwood supports routing policies. You can configure strict residency policies that prevent cross-region fallback, or looser ones that allow fallback to a compatible EU model variant in another EU zone. We can enforce a hard block so requests never cross the EU boundary if that's your requirement.
[04:15] Samir Rao: And if a region is down, will requests queue or fail? We need documented SLOs and behaviors.
[04:21] Maya Patel: We have configurable fallback: canary rollouts, queueing, or immediate failure. For mission-critical financial flows we recommend Dedicated with burst capacity and an SLA-backed throughput; for extra control Private with customer-managed network and explicit playbooks is safest.
[04:36] Leah Ortiz: Okay, next: logs access control. Our security team demands RBAC and SSO/SAML integration so only named people can retrieve logs. Is that available?
[04:44] Maya Patel: Yes — Redwood Console supports RBAC, SSO via SAML/OIDC, and audit trails for log access. You can also push logs to your own SIEM in near real time and keep the retention there.
[04:55] Daniel Knox: Who can see unredacted prompts in your stack? Is it accessible by Redwood ops for debugging?
[05:01] Maya Patel: Access to unredacted prompts is strictly limited. For Hosted we have a small ops team with audited access; for Dedicated and Private you can opt out of any Redwood-side prompt retention and require debug bundles to be delivered to you only. We'll generate ephemeral debug keys if needed.
[05:15] Samir Rao: Are you able to produce evidence of log deletion and retention policy enforcement? We will need proof for audits.
[05:22] Alex Chen: We provide audit logs showing retention lifecycle events and deletion timestamps. We can also provide an ingestion-to-deletion flow diagram as part of the evidence package.
[05:30] Priya Singh: What about model artifacts and token caching? We use KV cache in our embeddings flow, will those entries be considered data retention?
[05:40] Maya Patel: Cache is configurable — prefix and KV cache can be ephemeral or persisted depending on your policy. For compliance-sensitive workloads we set short TTLs or disable persistent cache. We can also encrypt caches with your keys.
[05:52] Leah Ortiz: There are some tricky product requirements — we need to allow user requests from an EU office but allow some processing in the US for internal analytics, but only if PII is removed. Is it possible to split pipelines so redaction happens in EU and non-PII telemetry goes to the US?
[06:07] Maya Patel: Yes that's a common pattern. You can run an EU pre-processing step that strips or tokenizes PII, then forward sanitized telemetry to global analytics. Redwood routing can help; we can propose a pipeline where call-level telemetry (sans prompts) goes out, while content stays resident.
[06:22] Samir Rao: How deterministic is your PII detection for non-English inputs? We have customers in multiple EU languages.
[06:29] Maya Patel: It's harder in non-English; our scrubbing uses multi-lingual heuristics and token classification models. We'll want to run a short evaluation over your corpus. That will be part of the SE deep dive.
[06:40] Alex Chen: Quick clarification — you mentioned 7-year retention for some logs, is that for regulatory retention or legal hold?
[06:47] Daniel Knox: Both. Some records need 7 years for regulatory, and legal hold might be indefinite. So we need a way to put certain items into long-term retention while others expire.
[06:56] Maya Patel: We support retention segmentation and legal hold markers. Legal hold suspends deletion for specified resource ids and we can export the legal-hold artifacts to your storage.
[07:07] Leah Ortiz: Another ask — we need a workflow for redaction review. Compliance will sometimes request a human review of a redaction to verify no PHI got through. How does that work without exposing raw data widely?
[07:18] Maya Patel: We can provide a controlled audit UI where redactions are staged and only authorized auditors can see ephemeral unredacted views; everything is logged. Alternatively, you can set up an export of flagged items to your secure enclave for review.
[07:33] Samir Rao: For performance — dedicated vs hosted — what's the expected latency delta? Our SLAs are tight for customer chat.
[07:40] Maya Patel: Hosted in-region typically gives lowest time-to-market, Dedicated removes noisy neighbors and gives more predictable latency. Latency variance with Dedicated is lower; if you need absolute strict p95 numbers we can run a benchmark with similar prompt lengths.
[07:53] Alex Chen: Competitors we've seen — teams sometimes build in-house GPU endpoints, or use Vertex/Anthropic. Main differentiator is Redwood's routing and observability plus the ability to run Private deployments.
[08:04] Leah Ortiz: Pricing is also a factor — for sustained high volume, Dedicated makes economic sense. But procurement asks for an annual contract and pricing model.
[08:12] Alex Chen: We'll follow up with pricing for Dedicated and a comparison sheet that maps hosted costs to Dedicated committed rates.
[08:19] Priya Singh: We also need a test plan: sample dataset, performance targets, and security acceptance criteria.
[08:25] Maya Patel: We'll propose a pilot — a four-week dedicated trial in EU with X GPUs, run your prompt set and retention rules, and produce an evidence pack.
[08:36] Samir Rao: On the topic of PII in logs — does Redwood compress or obfuscate token data at rest? Is it searchable?
[08:42] Maya Patel: Token-level traces can be stored encrypted; searchable fields are metadata only unless you opt-in. We can encrypt the full prompt store with your key and restrict search. Searchable fields like hashed user id and route are available for observability.
[08:56] Leah Ortiz: Great. Any gotchas about legal holds across our subsidiaries? We have a US entity and an EU entity — sometimes data must remain where it was created.
[09:05] Maya Patel: That is solvable with tenant partitioning and region locks. You may want separate tenants per legal entity to keep evidence separated.
[09:14] Daniel Knox: One more: we may need deep forensics for incident response — logs with full prompt snapshots for a bounded timeframe. Can Redwood produce point-in-time exports?
[09:24] Maya Patel: Yes, we can create time-bounded export bundles. For Hosted we require a request and ephemeral access; for Dedicated/Private you can host export endpoints yourself. All access is auditable.
[09:35] Alex Chen: Okay, sounds like the pattern is: we can meet the requirements; next steps are artifacts and a SE-run pilot. I'll summarize and send links.
[09:44] Samir Rao: Cool. Quick question — do you support hardware attestations (SGX/TEE) or HSM attestation for keys?
[09:51] Maya Patel: We support HSM-backed KMS and can provide attestation statements when keys are in your HSM. TEEs like SGX are on the roadmap but not generally available across all models.
[10:03] Priya Singh: Can you capture the key flow? I'd like a sequence diagram for how keys are used for encrypting caches, prompts, and logs.
[10:11] Maya Patel: We'll include a sequence diagram in the artifacts pack.
[10:16] Leah Ortiz: Are you able to redact logs at regex-level and also at semantic-level with an LLM classifier? Which is recommended?
[10:24] Maya Patel: We do both — regex for deterministic patterns (PAN, SSNs) and semantic classifiers for free-form PII. For high-assurance workflows we suggest layered approach plus manual review for flagged items.
[10:36] Samir Rao: For long-term retention, we need proof-of-deletion when the retention window expires. You mentioned lifecycle events. Can those be exported to our SIEM?
[10:44] Maya Patel: Yes, lifecycle events and deletion notifications can be pushed to your SIEM or audit bucket.
[10:49] Alex Chen: Great — we're at about 10 minutes into the call. Any other blocking concerns?
[10:55] Daniel Knox: Not blocking, but procurement will ask for minimum commitments and break clauses for Dedicated. We'll need those terms.
[11:03] Alex Chen: Understood — we'll include contract terms in the follow-up with procurement.
[11:08] Priya Singh: One tiny detail: are inference logs ever used to improve Redwood models? We cannot have customer prompt material used in model training.
[11:16] Maya Patel: By default no customer prompts are used for training without explicit opt-in. We have a strict policy; we can provide that in writing.
[11:24] Leah Ortiz: Perfect. Okay, let's recap next steps.

Action Items (verbal):
[11:30] Alex Chen: I'll send SOC2, security deck, and a redacted network diagram by 2028-10-06.
[11:33] Maya Patel: I'll draft a pilot plan and Dedicated sizing proposal by 2028-10-09 and prepare a SE deep dive for your infra team.
[11:39] Priya Singh: We'll share sample prompts and a list of PII patterns to test by 2028-10-08.
[11:43] Samir Rao: We'll review the artifacts and confirm whether we need Private or Dedicated for initial pilot.

[11:48] Alex Chen: Anything else from the team?
[11:51] Daniel Knox: No, thanks. This was useful.
[11:53] Leah Ortiz: Good session. We'll talk after we review the materials.
[11:57] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites.
[12:00] (call ends)

References mentioned:

Notes on transcript quality: some acronyms and technical terms may be mis-transcribed (K V cache as K-V cash, VPC heard as V P C), speaker labels auto-attributed in places.
